::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[How to do root test on this power series?](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/4548269/how-to-do-root-test-on-this-power-series), asked by [Hamsa Ahmed Mohamed](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/866312/hamsa-ahmed-mohamed) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2022-10-08; [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)):

> I have this power series,
>
> $$\sum_{n=2}^{\infty} \frac{x^{n}}{\ln (n)}, \quad x \in \mathbb{R},$$
>
> I apply the root test as such,
> $$\sum_{n=2}^{\infty} \frac{x^{n}}{\ln (n)}=\lim_{n \to \infty } \left(  \frac{x^{n}}{\ln (n)} \right)^{\frac{1}{n}}= \frac{x}{\ln(n)^{\frac{1}{n}}}$$
>
> And Wolfram tells me when,
>
> $$\lim_{n \to \infty } \sqrt[n]{\ln(n)} = 1$$
> Firstly how do I prove that's true?
> Secondly How I interpet this?
> $$\sum_{n=2}^{\infty} \frac{x^{n}}{\ln (n)}=\lim_{n \to \infty } \left(  \frac{x^{n}}{\ln (n)} \right)^{\frac{1}{n}}= \frac{x}{1}= x$$
:::

You are correct that $$\lim_{n\to\infty} \left|\frac{x^n}{\ln x}\right|^{1/n} = |x|$$To show that $(\ln n)^{1/n} \to 1$, start with the fact that $$\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{\ln n}{n} = 0$$ to show that $1 < \ln n < n$ eventually for all $n$. Then take $n$th roots and limits.

The [root test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Root_test) says that the series converges absolutely if this limit is less than $1$, and diverges if the limit is greater than $1$.

So now you know the series converges absolutely if $|x|<1$, and diverges if $|x|>1$. That is, the radius of convergence of this power series is $1$.
